title: When Training Becomes a Catch-All for Something Else
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez argues that organizations use the word training as shorthand for a much broader set of needs, from process problems to new systems to unclear expectations. Because training is a comfortable, tangible solution that lets a team build a course and check a box, leaders reach for it before diagnosing what actually needs to change. She offers a richer vocabulary that separates training, enablement, communications, knowledge management, change management, organizational development and process or system design. A learning team may be competent to contribute to all of these, but she distinguishes competence from capacity and authority, since the ability to do something does not make a team the right owner or mean it is resourced for it. She closes with a diagnostic list that maps what people know and can do to the right kind of opportunity, from learning to process, technology, role clarity, alignment or strategy.
points: Calling every organizational problem a training need hides the real scope of the work and leads to underestimating the time, expertise and coordination required.
Training, enablement, communications, knowledge management, change management, organizational development and process design are different disciplines that are not interchangeable.
A team being able to contribute to a problem is not the same as being the right function to own it, so expertise, authority and capacity all matter.
The intervention should match the scope of the change, and ongoing support in the flow of work needs infrastructure beyond a one-time training event.
A simple diagnostic sorts problems by what people know and can do, which points to a learning, process, technology, ownership, alignment or strategy response.
quotes: Training is a comfortable mental model. It’s also a tangible solution. You can build a course, schedule a webinar, create a guide, and check a box.

A process isn’t working, so we need training. A new system is launching, so we need training. People don’t know where to find information, so we need training. Expectations are inconsistent, so we need training.
But being able to contribute to something isn’t the same as being the right function to own it. There are questions of expertise. There are questions of authority.
We identify something a team can do and then this turns into something the team should do. But there’s a difference between competence and capacity.

Naming all of this “training” can overshadow the many resources necessary to solve the issue at hand. Because when we don’t see the full scope of the work, we’re much more likely to underestimate the time, expertise, people, and cross-functional coordination required to do it effectively.
And sometimes the most valuable thing a learning professional can do is recognize that the problem in front of us isn’t actually a learning problem at all.
Organizations get better outcomes when they diagnose the problem first and then determine the right intervention, expertise, ownership, and resourcing.
